tur41-0: What is shoulder impingement (subacromial pain, rotator cuff tendinitis), how is it recognised, does a tear on an MRI matter, and is surgery needed? A comparison of the 2025 guidelines, a short history, six home exercises, videos and warning signs.
tur41-1: It shows up as pain on the outer side of the shoulder, sometimes spreading down the arm, when you lift the arm out to the side or overhead. It was once thought that something was being "pinched" between the bones; today the focus is on the tendons of the muscles that rotate the shoulder (the rotator cuff) and the structures around them. Exercise is the cornerstone of treatment; surgery is usually not needed.
tur41-2: People found to have a full-thickness tendon tear in a community screening; two-thirds of these tears caused no symptoms
tur41-3: At follow-up, decompression surgery was no better than sham surgery or exercise
tur41-4: Time within which most symptoms are expected to respond (BESS)
tur41-7: The narrow space between the bony roof on top of the shoulder (the acromion) and the upper arm bone is called the subacromial space. It contains the tendons of the muscles that rotate the shoulder (the rotator cuff) and a fluid-filled sac (bursa). Excessive or unaccustomed loading of these structures can cause pain.
tur41-8: It used to be thought that the tendon was being "pinched" against the bone. Today it is thought that the pain often cannot be explained by a single mechanical pinch, and that the tendon's response to load also plays a part; this is why the names "subacromial pain" and "rotator cuff related shoulder pain" are also used.
tur41-9: Risk factors: increasing age (most common in people in their 50s), jobs and sports in which the arm is used repeatedly or for long periods above head height
tur41-10: Shoulder impingement is a clinical diagnosis: it is made from your history and an examination, and imaging is not needed to confirm it or to start treatment. The neck is also checked during the examination, because pain coming from the neck can be felt in the shoulder.
tur41-12: Pain within a certain range when lifting the arm out to the side (a painful arc) supports the diagnosis. No pain on the Hawkins-Kennedy test (the arm is raised forward and, with the elbow bent, turned inwards) makes shoulder impingement less likely. No single test is enough on its own; the tests are interpreted together.
tur41-14: Usually not at the first assessment. If imaging is needed, ultrasound is the first choice; the JOSPT guideline recommends it for people who have not improved despite about 12 weeks of properly delivered treatment, and does not recommend MRI routinely. An X-ray may be requested after an injury, when there are warning signs, when pain or stiffness is very severe, or when symptoms have lasted a long time.
tur41-16: Shoulder pain has other causes too: frozen shoulder, calcium deposits in a tendon, shoulder arthritis, large tendon tears, shoulder dislocation or instability, and pain coming from the neck. The examination helps tell these apart.
tur41-18: In a study in which Japanese researchers screened 664 people in a village with ultrasound, one in five (22.1%) had a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, and two-thirds of these tears caused no symptoms. Tears become more common with age: from 10.7% of people in their 50s to 36.6% of those in their 80s.
tur41-19: From the idea of "impingement" to exercise
tur41-20: For about half a century, the bone rubbing against the tendon was seen as the cause of shoulder pain, and surgery to shave the bone was widely performed. Trials comparing it with sham surgery have seriously called this approach into question.
tur41-21: The surgeon Neer proposed that the front part of the bony roof on top of the shoulder (the acromion), together with a ligament attached to it (the coracoacromial ligament), rubs against the tendons of the muscles that rotate the shoulder. He wrote that this produces a characteristic picture (impingement syndrome) and recommended, as treatment, removing the front edge and underside of the bony roof together with this ligament.
tur41-22: In a randomised trial of 140 patients, surgery to shave the bony roof followed by exercise added no benefit for pain at 2 years over a supervised exercise programme alone; it was, however, considerably more costly.
tur41-23: A review article used the name "rotator cuff related shoulder pain". This name describes the pain without tying it to a single mechanical "impingement".
tur41-24: In the CSAW trial of 313 patients at 32 hospitals in the United Kingdom, decompression surgery showed no clinically meaningful difference at 6 months or 1 year compared with sham (placebo) surgery in which the inside of the joint was only looked at with a camera.
tur41-25: In the FIMPACT trial of 210 patients at three hospitals in Finland, decompression surgery gave no better results at 2 years than arthroscopy done only for diagnosis. The 5-year results published in 2021 were the same: surgery was better than neither sham surgery nor exercise.
tur41-26: A Cochrane review of 8 trials and 1,062 people showed with high certainty that decompression surgery gives no clinically important benefit over sham surgery for pain, function or quality of life. In the same year an international expert panel (BMJ) made a strong recommendation against this operation.
tur41-27: Two new sources were published: a guideline (JOSPT) prepared by an international expert group and also supported by the orthopaedic academy of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA), and the patient care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS). Both put exercise as the first step of treatment.
tur41-28: Guidelines put exercise at the centre of treatment; other methods are used as support to make exercise possible. According to the 2025 care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS), this condition often tends to settle on its own and most symptoms respond within 3 months; if there is no improvement by 12 weeks, specialist assessment is recommended.
tur41-29: Learning what the pain is, how it is likely to progress and how to adjust daily activities is part of treatment.
tur41-30: It is the cornerstone of treatment. A programme that strengthens the shoulder and shoulder blade muscles, with the load increased gradually, reduces pain and improves function. For results, the programme needs to be kept up regularly for weeks. The best type and dose of exercise are not yet known; the programme is tailored to the person.
tur41-32: Manual therapy can be used together with exercise to reduce pain in the short term. Studies on the benefit of taping are conflicting; it can be tried as short-term extra support. Neither is a treatment on its own.
tur41-34: Shockwave and laser may be considered mainly in people with calcium deposits in the tendon (weak recommendation); without calcium deposits, shockwave is not recommended. Ultrasound therapy is not recommended because it has shown no benefit. Calcium deposits in the shoulder →

Surgical assessment is a separate matter for large tendon tears caused by an injury.

Details of the JOSPT guideline were taken from secondary summaries; treatment is chosen for each person.

If pain increases in the exercises where you lift your arm, make the range of movement smaller.

Push outwards against the door frame with the back of your hand, without your arm moving. Hold for 30–45 seconds with a force that does not increase pain.

Lower slowly without hunching your shoulders up towards your ears.
tur41-67: Most people improve clearly with non-surgical treatment; however, in some people symptoms can last for months or come back. According to the 2025 care pathway of the British Elbow and Shoulder Society (BESS), most symptoms usually respond within 3 months; if there is no improvement by 12 weeks, specialist assessment is recommended. An exercise programme with gradually increasing load is the cornerstone of treatment.
tur41-68: Usually not. Decompression surgery, which shaves away the bony spur, was not found to be better than sham or purely diagnostic surgery in two large trials, and an international expert panel recommends against it. BESS also does not recommend surgery as a first-line treatment; it states that it may be considered in some people who have not improved despite 6 months of non-surgical treatment, but that there are no reliable criteria for telling who will benefit. If you cannot lift your arm after an injury such as a fall, surgical assessment is needed separately.
tur41-69: Seeing a tear is not a reason for worry on its own. In a community screening that Japanese researchers carried out with ultrasound in a village, one in five people had a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, and two-thirds of these tears caused no symptoms. Treatment decisions are based on your symptoms and examination findings, not on the MRI image. If there is clear weakness, or if the tear occurred after a fall or blow, your physician may ask for a surgical assessment.
tur41-70: A cortisone injection can reduce pain, but the effect is temporary (usually less than 12 weeks), and adding it to exercise made no extra difference in the long term. The 2025 guidelines do not recommend it as a first-line treatment; repeat injections have not been shown to add benefit over a single injection. You can make the decision together with your physician.
tur41-71: Do I need an MRI or ultrasound scan?
tur41-72: Usually not at the start; the diagnosis is made from your history and an examination. According to the JOSPT guideline, if there is no improvement despite about 12 weeks of properly delivered treatment, ultrasound is the first choice and MRI is not recommended routinely (expert opinion). BESS also regards ultrasound by an experienced operator as the first choice if imaging is needed. An X-ray may be requested after an injury, if there are warning signs, if pain or stiffness is very severe, or if symptoms have lasted a long time.

tur41-80: What is hip osteoarthritis (coxarthrosis), how is it diagnosed, does an X-ray explain the pain, and why can the pain be felt in the knee? The real effect of exercise, a comparison of the ACR and NICE guidelines, a short history, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur41-81: It develops as the cartilage in the hip joint gradually thins. The pain is usually felt in the groin; putting on socks, tying shoelaces and getting into a car can become harder. Exercise, losing weight if you are overweight and, when needed, aids such as a walking stick can make daily life easier; if pain and limitation are very marked, hip replacement is an option.

tur41-97: Hip replacement, which became widespread in the 1960s, turned into a life-changing treatment for advanced osteoarthritis. In recent years, research has shown more clearly the place and the limits of exercise and of understanding the condition well in the period before surgery.
tur41-98: In England, the surgeon John Charnley introduced into practice the total hip replacement operation he had developed at Wrightington Hospital. A year earlier he had presented the method in The Lancet as "a new operation".

These criteria were developed to classify patients in research.
tur41-100: A review published in The Lancet described total hip replacement as "the operation of the century".

tur41-137: According to the Cochrane review updated in 2026 (18 trials, 1,368 people), exercise probably reduces pain in hip osteoarthritis by about 7 points more out of 100 than no treatment or usual care (moderate-certainty evidence); this is below the 12 points usually considered noticeable in daily life (this threshold comes mostly from knee studies). A similar small improvement is seen in function. The Cochrane authors say that exercise is low-cost, unlikely to cause harm and good for general health, so it keeps its place in treatment. The American College of Rheumatology also strongly recommends exercise in its 2019 guideline, published before this review. Exercise is part of a treatment package together with weight management, a walking stick and understanding the condition well. The UK's 2022 guideline (NICE) also recommends exercise tailored to the person for everyone and weight loss for those who are overweight (even a small amount of weight loss is probably beneficial), and states that walking aids such as a walking stick may be considered if needed, that imaging is usually not needed for diagnosis, and that glucosamine and strong opioids are not recommended. In an umbrella review published in 2026, combining 5 systematic reviews and 28 randomised trials, the effect of exercise on hip pain was of a similar size to the Cochrane estimate, but these authors describe the effect as negligible; they recommend shared decision-making that does not overlook the general health benefits of exercise and patients' preferences.

Hip pain can also have other causes, such as the lower back, hip impingement or tendon problems; an assessment is needed.

tur41-156: What is carpal tunnel syndrome, how is it recognised, does it go away on its own, and can using a computer cause it? Night splints, a comparison of the AAOS and physiotherapy guidelines, a short history, four home exercises and warning signs.
tur41-157: It occurs when the median nerve is compressed in a narrow channel in the wrist (the carpal tunnel). It causes numbness, tingling and pain in the thumb, index and middle fingers; symptoms are typically worse at night. In mild to moderate cases, a night splint and adjusting daily load are the first step; in cases that do not settle or that progress, the nerve can be relieved with a minor operation.
tur41-158: People with numbness, tingling or pain in the median nerve area (a community study of adults aged 25–74 in Sweden, 1999)
tur41-160: Time a night splint may need before it starts to help (NHS)
tur41-161: Does it go away on its own?
tur41-163: If the nerve stays markedly compressed for a long time, the numbness can become permanent and the muscles at the base of the thumb can weaken; this is why worsening symptoms should be assessed.
tur41-164: The diagnosis is mostly based on where and when the symptoms occur and on an examination. Marking on a hand diagram which parts of the hand are affected also helps the assessment.
tur41-166: Six findings are assessed together: numbness mainly in the fingers supplied by the median nerve, numbness at night, wasting or weakness of the muscles at the base of the thumb, a positive Phalen test, reduced ability to tell two points apart, and a positive Tinel sign. The 2024 AAOS guideline states that this score can be used instead of routine EMG or ultrasound. It is a tool used during an examination, not for self-diagnosis.
tur41-167: In the Phalen test the wrists are held bent for 30–60 seconds; in the Tinel test the palm side of the wrist is tapped lightly. The test is positive if numbness or tingling appears in the fingers. No test is accurate enough on its own; the findings are interpreted together.
tur41-168: When are EMG and ultrasound needed?
tur41-169: Nerve conduction studies and EMG, or ultrasound, are not needed for every patient. They are requested when the diagnosis is uncertain or when the result would change treatment (for example, the decision about surgery). According to AAOS, MRI should not be used for diagnosis.
tur41-170: In some people it can improve on its own. In a study that followed 196 untreated patients (274 hands) for 10–15 months, symptoms and nerve measurements generally improved on their own; however, measurements worsened in those whose findings were mild at the start. A short duration of symptoms and younger age were linked with a better course; symptoms in both hands and a positive Phalen test were linked with a worse course.
tur41-171: In pregnancy: Symptoms usually ease after giving birth as the swelling goes down. However, in a study that followed 45 women, about half still had symptoms 3 years after giving birth (only one had needed surgery). This is why symptoms that do not go away after birth should also be assessed.
tur41-172: The expert group that prepared the 2024 guideline of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), noting the lack of reliable research, holds the view that heavy keyboard use is not linked with carpal tunnel syndrome; this is the lowest level of evidence in the guideline. The 2026 physiotherapy guideline gives a weak recommendation for options such as keyboards that need less force, touch screens, or switching the mouse between hands in people with symptoms.
tur41-174: A short history of carpal tunnel syndrome
tur41-175: Nerve compression at the wrist has been known for about 170 years, but the condition only became widely recognised in the middle of the 20th century. In recent years, research has shown more clearly the place of splints, injections and surgery.
tur41-176: James Paget described two cases of median nerve compression at the wrist: in one, a cord tied tightly around the wrist, and in the other, excess bone formed after a wrist fracture, was pressing on the nerve.
tur41-177: Pierre Marie and Charles Foix described wasting of the muscles at the base of the thumb caused by involvement of the median nerve at the level of the ligament in the wrist, and suggested that early division of this ligament might prevent progression.
tur41-178: The first carpal tunnel release operation is reported to have been performed by Herbert Galloway.
tur41-179: Brain, Wright and Wilkinson showed that the median nerve can be compressed at the wrist even without an obvious external cause, leading to sensory disturbance and wasting of the thumb muscles; they reported six cases treated with surgery.
tur41-180: George Phalen clarified the diagnosis and treatment of the condition through large series of patients and brought it wide recognition. The Phalen test, done by holding the wrists bent, bears his name. The name "carpal tunnel syndrome" was first used in a 1953 publication by Kremer.

tur41-218: Hold your hand upright with your fingers straight. Move through the following positions in turn, holding each for 5 seconds: keeping the knuckles at the base of the fingers straight, bend the middle and end joints to make a hook; make a full fist; keep your fingers straight and bend them only at the base knuckles to 90 degrees (tabletop position); make a fist with the fingertips staying straight; then open your hand. It helps the finger tendons glide easily through the tunnel. Stop if your symptoms get worse.
tur41-220: Stand upright and hold your arm out to the side, a little below shoulder height, with your palm facing up; your elbow can be slightly bent. As you slowly bend your wrist back, tilt your head towards the same side, towards your arm; as you release your wrist, bring your head back upright. This way the nerve is tightened at one end while it is slackened at the other, so it glides without being stretched. If tingling or numbness increases, make the movement smaller or stop.
tur41-221: Hold your arm out in front of you with the elbow straight and palm facing up. With your other hand, gently pull your fingers down and back; feel a mild stretch on the inner side of your forearm. You can start with your elbow slightly bent; stop if tingling starts.
tur41-222: Place your hand on a table, palm facing up. With your other hand, gently open your thumb outwards and backwards; feel a mild stretch at the base of the thumb. Do not force it if the joint at the base of your thumb hurts.
tur41-223: When symptoms start, shaking your hand and changing position may bring relief.
tur41-224: In some people it can improve on its own. In a study that followed 196 untreated patients (274 hands) for 10–15 months, symptoms and nerve measurements generally improved on their own; however, measurements worsened in those whose findings were mild at the start. A short duration of symptoms and younger age were linked with a better course, while symptoms in both hands and a positive Phalen test were linked with a worse course. With long-lasting or steadily increasing numbness and weakness, treatment should not be delayed, so that the nerve is not permanently damaged.
tur41-225: A splint that keeps the wrist straight is worn mainly at night. According to England's National Health Service (NHS), a splint may take up to 6 weeks to help. According to the 2026 physiotherapy guideline, if a night splint is not enough, wearing it during the day too or changing the splint's position may be considered; decide this together with your physiotherapist.
tur41-226: The expert group that prepared the 2024 guideline of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), noting the lack of reliable research, holds the view that heavy keyboard use is not linked with carpal tunnel syndrome; this is the lowest level of evidence in the guideline. In the 2016 AAOS guideline, by contrast, computer work was listed among the risk factors. According to the NHS, jobs involving repeated gripping, excess weight and pregnancy are among the risk factors.
tur41-227: A cortisone injection can reduce symptoms quickly: in a study of 234 people, a single injection gave more relief than a night splint at 6 weeks; by 6 months there was no difference between the groups. According to the 2024 AAOS guideline, cortisone injections have no long-term benefit; symptoms can return over time. You can make the decision together with your physician.
tur41-228: If there is thinning of the muscles at the base of the thumb, constant numbness, weakness, or symptoms that persist despite a splint and other treatments, an assessment by a hand surgeon is needed. According to the 2016 AAOS guideline, the benefit of surgery at 6 and 12 months is greater than that of non-surgical treatments. In a study of 176 patients in the Netherlands, success at 18 months was 90% in the surgery group and 75% in the splint group; however, 41% of the splint group had had surgery by then.
tur41-229: Tendon and nerve gliding exercises are widely used, but according to a Cochrane review the evidence for their effectiveness is limited and of very low quality; the 2026 physiotherapy guideline also makes no clear recommendation for these exercises. The guideline gives a weak recommendation for a stretching programme together with a splint in mild to moderate cases without wasting of the thumb-base muscles and with normal two-point discrimination. Exercises should be done as support for the splint and load adjustment, without increasing pain and numbness.
tur41-230: Does carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy go away after birth?
tur41-231: Symptoms usually ease after birth as the swelling goes down; during this period a night splint can be used until the hand returns to normal. However, in a study that followed 45 women, about half still had symptoms 3 years after giving birth; only one had needed surgery. If symptoms do not go away, assessment after birth is also important.
tur41-233: Not always. According to the 2024 AAOS guideline, the examination-based CTS-6 score can be used instead of routine EMG or ultrasound. A nerve conduction study is requested when the diagnosis is uncertain or when the result would change treatment (for example, the decision about surgery).

tur41-235: Go to the emergency department straight away or call 112:
tur41-236: Sudden weakness of the arm or face, numbness, difficulty speaking (it may be a stroke; call 112)
tur41-237: Rapidly increasing numbness, swelling and severe pain after a wrist injury or fracture
tur41-238: Redness, warmth and swelling in the wrist together with a fever
tur41-239: Numbness spreading into the arm together with neck pain (it may come from the neck)
tur41-240: Numbness in both hands and the legs, clumsy hands or unsteadiness when walking (it may come from the spinal cord or a nerve disease; if there are problems with bladder or bowel control, go to the emergency department)
